readings.c1s1:
¶
'''trashily''' (trash′i-li), ''adv.'' In a trashy manner.

'''trashiness''' (trash′i-nes), ''n.'' The state or property of being trashy.

'''trashtrie''' (trash′tri), ''n.'' [< ''trash''<sup>1</sup> + ''-trie'', ''-try'' for ''-ry''. Cf. ''trashery''.] Trash; worthless stuff.

{{smaller block|Wi' sauce, ragouts, and sic like ''trashtrie''.
{{right|''Burns'', The Twa Dogs.}}}}

'''trashy''' (trash′i), ''a.'' [< ''trash''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Composed of or resembling trash, rubbish, or dross; waste; worthless; useless.

{{smaller block|I am now buying books; not ''trashy'' books which will only bear one reading, but good books for a library.
{{right|''Macaulay'', in Trevelyan, I. 314.}}}}

'''Traskite''' (trȧsk′īt), ''n.'' [< ''Trask'' (see def.) + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] An early name of the Seventh-Day Baptists, from John Trask, one of their leaders in England in the seventeenth century. See ''Baptist''.

'''trass''' (tras), ''n.'' [< G. dial. ''trass'' = D. ''tras'' (''tiras'', ''tieras'') = E. ''terrace''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.] An earthy or more or less compact rock, made up in large part of firmly comminuted pumice or other volcanic material. {{smaller|It is of a pale-yellow or grayish color, and rough to the feel. Trass closely resembles pozzuolana, and like that is extensively used for hydraulic cement, especially by the Dutch engineers. It is largely quarried for that purpose along the Rhine, between Mainz and Cologne. Also ''terras''. See ''tuff''<sup>3</sup>.}}

'''trasse†''', '''trasshe†''', ''v.'' Middle English forms of ''traise''.

'''trast<sup>1</sup>†'''. An obsolete form of the past participle of ''trace''<sup>1</sup>. ''Spenser''.

'''trast<sup>2</sup>''', ''n.'' A Scotch form of ''trest''<sup>2</sup>.

'''trasy†''', ''n.'' A spaniel.
readings.c1s3:
{{smaller block|As for ae ae ae &c., I know not what other censure to pass on them but that they are childish and ridiculous ''traulisms.''
{{right|''Dalgarno,'' Deaf and Dumb Man's Tutor (1680), p. 132.}}}}

'''traul-net†''', ''n.'' Another spelling of ''trawl-net.'' See ''trawl,'' 2.

'''trauma''' (trâ′mä), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. τραῦμα, Ionic τρῶμα, wound, < τρώειν, pierce.] 1. An abnormal condition of the living body produced by external violence, as distinguished from that produced by poisons, zymotic infection, bad habits, and other less evident causes; traumatism; an accidental wound, as distinguished from one caused by the surgeon's knife in an operation.—2. External violence producing bodily injury; the act of wounding, or infliction of a wound.

'''traumatic''' (trâ-mat′ik), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [= F. ''traumatique,'' < Gr. τραυματικός, < τραῦμα(τ-), wound (see ''trauma''), + ''-ic.''] I. ''a.'' 1. Of or pertaining to wounds: as, ''traumatic'' inflammation.—2. Adapted to the cure of wounds; vulnerary: as, ''traumatic'' balsam.—3. Produced by wounds: as, ''traumatic'' tetanus.—4. Pertaining to or of the nature of trauma or traumatism.—'''Traumatic fever''', {{smaller|pyrexia caused by traumatism, especially where, as in simple fractures, it seems to be independent of infection.}}

II. ''n.'' A medicine useful in the cure of wounds.

'''traumatically''' (trâ-mat′i-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In a traumatic manner.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''traumaticin''' (trâ-mat′i-sin), ''n.'' [< ''traumatic'' + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.] A 10 per-cent. solution of gutta-percha in chloroform, employed like collodion to promote union of the edges of a wound.

'''traumatism''' (trâ′ma-tizm), ''n.'' [= F. ''traumatisme'', < Gr. τραῦμα(τ-), wound (see ''traumatic''), + ''-ism''.] Any morbid condition produced by wounds or other external violence; trauma.

'''traumatopnœa''' (trâ″ma-top-nē′ä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. τραῦμα(τ-), a wound, + πνοιή for πνοή, breath, < πνεῖν, blow, breathe.] Respiratory bubbling of air through a wound in the chest.

'''traunce†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''trance''<sup>1</sup>, ''trance''<sup>2</sup>.

'''traunch†''', ''v.'' An obsolete form of ''trench''.

'''traunt†''', '''traunter†'''. See ''trant'', ''tranter''.

'''Trautvetteria''' (trât-ve-tē′ri-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL. (Fischer and Meyer, 1835), named after E. R. ''Trautvetter'', professor of botany at Kieff, Russia.] A genus of plants, of the order ''Ranunculaceæ'' and tribe ''Ranunculeæ'', distinguished from the type, ''Ranunculus'', by the absence of petals.

{{smaller block|The only species, ''T. palmata'', the false bugbane, is a perennial herb, a native of North America and Japan, bearing a few palmately lobed leaves, and numerous small white flowers in a corymbose panicle. Compare ''bugbane''.}}

'''travail'''<sup>1</sup> (trav′āl), ''n.'' [An earlier form of ''travel'', now differentiated in a particular use (def. 2): see ''travel'', ''n.''] 1†. Labor; toil; travel: same as ''travel'', 1.—2. Labor in childbed; parturition. [Archaic.]

{{smaller block|In the time of her ''travail'', behold, . . . twins were in her womb.
{{right|Gen. xxxviii. 27.}}
After this thy ''travel'' sore,
Sweet rest seize thee evermore.
{{right|''Milton'', Epitaph on Marchioness of Winchester.}}}}

[Archaic.] {{smaller block|Noa. that relyques of the stones of the place there our Lady was borne is remedy and consolacion to women that ''trauayll'' of childe. {{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 30.}}}} {{smaller block|And when she heard the tidings . . . she bowed herself and ''travailed;'' for her pains came upon her. {{right|1 Sam. iv. 19.}}}} {{smaller block|Queen Jeanie ''travel'd'' six weeks and more, Till women and midwives had quite gi'en her o'er. {{right|''Queen Jeanie'' (Child's Ballads, VII. 75).}}}} '''travail2''' (F. pron. tra-vay′), ''n.''; F. pl. ''travaux'' (tra-vō′). [< F. ''travail'', a brake, trave, < ML. *''trabaculum'' (also, after Rom., ''trabale'', ''travallum''), a brake, shackle: see ''travel, n.''] A means of transportation, commonly used by North American Indians and voyageurs of the north and northwest, for the conveyance of goods or of sick or wounded persons. {{smaller|It consists of a rude litter made of two lodge-poles about 16 feet long, having one end of each pole attached on each side to a pack-saddle, the other end trailing on the ground. A kind of sack or bag is then made by lashing canvas or lodge-skins to the cross-bars, for the reception of the goods or the sick or wounded person. Also called ''travois'', ''travee''.}} [[File:century v08 p0248 c2f1.png|center|324px]] {{c|Travail, as used by the Sioux Indians.}} {{smaller block|In a month "Richard 's himself again," ready to fly over the grassy sward with his savage master, or to drag the ''travaux'' and pack the buxom squaw. {{right|''The Century'', XXXVII. 339.}}}} '''travailer†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''traveler''. '''travailous†''', ''a.'' See ''travelous''. '''travale''' (tra-val′), ''n.'' In ''tambourine-playing'', an effect produced by rubbing the wetted finger across the head of the instrument. The ''double travale'' is simply the same effect made twice as rapidly as usual. '''trave''' (trāv), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''treve''; < ME. ''trave'', < OF. ''traf'', ''tref'', ''trief'', a cross-beam, a brake, shackle, = Pr. ''trau'' = Sp. ''trabe'', ''traba'' = Pg. ''trava'', ''trave'' = It. ''trave'', < L. ''trabs'', ''trabis'', a beam. Hence ult. ''travail''1, ''travel''.] 1. A cross-beam; a beam or timber-work crossing a building. {{smaller block|The Ceilings and ''Traves'' are, after the Turkish manner, richly Painted and Guilded. {{right|''Maundrell'', Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 125.}}}} 2. A kind of shackle for a horse that is being taught to amble or pace. {{smaller block|She sproong as a colt doth in the ''trave''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Miller's Tale, l. 96.}}}} Also ''travis''. '''rave†''' (trāv), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''traven''; < ''trave'', ''n.''] To cross; thwart; run counter to. {{smaller block|This traytoure ''traues'' vs alway.{{right|''York Plays'', p. 381.}}}} '''travee''' (tra-vē′), ''n.'' Same as ''travail''2. '''travel''' (trav′el), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''travail'' (still retained archaically in one sense); < ME. ''travel'', ''travail'', ''travayl'', ''traveile'', ''traveyle'', < OF. ''travail'', F. ''travail'', labor, toil, work, trouble, a brake, shackle, = Pr. ''trabalh'', ''trebalh'', ''trebail'' = Sp. ''trabajo'' = Pg. ''trabalho'' = It. ''travaglio'' (''trabajo''), an obstacle, impediment, OIt. ''travaglio'', pen for cattle, ox-stall, < ML. *''travaculum'', *''trabaculum'' (also, after Rom., ''trabale'', ''travallum''), a brake, shackle, impediment, < *''travare'', *''trabare'' (> Pr. ''travar'' = F. ''en-traver''), impede, hinder, shackle, fetter, < L. ''trabs'', a beam: see ''trave''. Cf. ''embarrass'', as connected with ''bar''1.] 1†. Labor; toil; effort. {{smaller block|Ine huet [what] ''trauail'' he heth yleued, hou he heth his time uorlore [wasted]. {{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 130.}} He was wery for ''traveile'' of yevinge of strokes and receivinge. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 629.}} Generally all warlike people are a little idle, and love danger better than ''travail''. {{right|''Bacon'', True Greatness of Kingdoms (ed. 1887).}} I am grieved for you
That any chance of mine should thus defeat
Your (I must needs say) most deserving ''travails''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, v. 1.}} Who having never before eyed me, but only heard the common report of my virtue, learning, and ''travel''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia's Revels, iv. 1.}}}} 2. The act of traveling or journeying; particularly, a journeying to distant countries: as, he is much improved by ''travel''; he started on his ''travels''. {{smaller block|''Travel'', in the younger sort, is a part of education; in the elder, a part of experience. {{right|''Bacon'', ''Travel'' (ed. 1887).}}}} {{smaller block|I cannot rest from ''travel''; I will drink Life to the lees. {{right|''Tennyson'', Ulysses.}}}} {{smaller block|When ''travel'' has become a memory, all the richness of it rises to the surface like cream. {{right|''C. W. Stoddard'', Mashallah, p. 204.}}}} 3. ''pl.'' An account of occurrences and observations made during a journey; a book that relates one's experiences in traveling: as, ''travels'' in Italy: formerly in the singular. {{smaller block|The Voiage and ''Travaile'' of Sir John Maundevile, Kt., which treateth of the way to Hierusalem, and of Marvayles of Inde. {{right|''Mandeville'', ''Travels'', Title.}}}} {{smaller block|Histories . . . engage the soul by a variety of sensible occurrences; . . . voyages and ''travels'', and accounts of strange countries, . . . will assist in this work [of fixing the attention]. {{right|''Watts'', Improvement of Mind, i. 15.}}}} 4. Progress; going; movement. {{smaller block|Thus thou mayest, in two or three hours' ''travel'' over a few leaves, see and know that which cost him that writ it years, and travel over sea and land, before he knew it. {{right|''W. Wood'', quoted in Tyler's Amer. Lit., I. 172.}}}} {{smaller block|The more the variety of characters is multiplied, the more ''travel'' of the compositor's hand over the cases is necessary for picking them up, and by so much is the speed of his work retarded. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIII. 701.}}}} 5. In ''mech.'', the length of stroke of any moving part: as, the ''travel'' of the bed of a planer; the ''travel'' of a pendulum. Also called ''excursion.'' {{smaller block|The ''travel'' of each valve is 5¼ in., and can be varied by means of slotted levers on the reversing shaft. {{right|''The Engineer'', LXV. 388.}}}} {{smaller block|The great fault of this gun [a central-fire hammerless gun] is the difficulty in manipulating it, on account of the enormous ''travel'' required by the lever. {{right|''W. W. Greener'', The Gun, p. 325.}}}} 6. The passage or concourse of travelers; persons traveling: as, the ''travel'' was very heavy on outgoing trains and boats. [Colloq.]—7†. Labor in childbirth. See ''travail''1, 2. [Archaic.] {{smaller|=Syn. 2. ''Voyage, Tour'', etc. See ''journey''.}} '''travel''' (trav′el), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''traveled, travelled'', ppr. ''traveling, travelling''. [Formerly also ''travail'' (still retained archaically in one sense); < ME. ''travelen, travaillen, travayllen, traveylen'', < OF. ''travailler'', F. ''travailler'' = Pr. ''trebalhar, trebailhar'' = Sp. ''trabajar, trabalhar'' = Pg. ''trabalhar'' = It. ''travagliare'', labor, toil, etc.; from the noun.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' 1†. To labor; toil. {{smaller block|According as it was committed unto us, we have diligently ''travailed'' in this present visitation of the university. {{right|Quoted in ''J. Bradford's'' Works (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 369.}}}} {{smaller block|If we labour to maintain truth and reason, let not any think that we ''travel'' about a matter not needful. {{right|''Hooker.''}}}} 2. To pass or make a journey from place to place, whether on foot, on horseback, or in any conveyance, as a carriage or a ship; go to or visit distant or foreign places; journey: as, to ''travel'' for health or for pleasure. {{smaller block|For the Marchauntes come not thidre so comounly for to bye Marchandises as thei don in the Lond of the gret Chane; for it is to fer to ''travaylle'' to. ''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 270.}} {{smaller block|A wench That ''travels'' with her buttermilk to market Between two dorsers. {{right|''Shirley and Chapman'', The Ball, iv.}}}}
